lines: it so happens that I'm here unofficially I mean I'm I'm here but I'm not here to participate in an official visit to Indonesia but to participate in a discussion about freedom of expression and religion involving experts and activists from across South and Southeast Asia I'm not here either

tonight or throughout this week to speak about human rights and freedom of expression in Indonesia in particular and I wanted to make that clear right at the beginning but I have to admit that I would welcome the opportunity for a formal official visit to this great nation Special Rapporteurs conduct country visits around the world in which

I in my own role explore freedom of opinion and expression issues with government civil society academics and others we can only do so on the basis of invitations from governments which we seek through formal diplomatic requests i have actually requested such an invitation from the government of indonesia and it is my hope that i'll be

in a position to conduct an official visit and deepen my understanding of Indonesia's implementation of its obligations under human rights law in the near future tonight however I want to talk more generally about the freedom of expression and with apologies to the vast majority of you who have deep

knowledge and understanding of the right to freedom of opinion and expression I want to do some things that seem rather basic you know eventually we might get I hope perhaps in the QA to discussions that get more in depth about freedom of expression particularly in a digital age but I want to speak a little bit more generally so first what I want to do is say a few words about the underlying law

that protects everyone's right to freedom of expression second i will sis i will suggest a kind of basic foundation for the law itself why did states after all agreed to protect opinion and expression what interests and policies to such protection serve third I'll address what I see as the worldwide threat to freedom of expression and and I have to say it's not monolithic it's

not based on one principle or one kind of threat it is not only online but it's offline it is not only driven by governments though that is often the case but it also results from social cultural political and demographic pressures worldwide I will spend a bit of time talking about content-based restrictions or discrimination and then

I'll talk about the tools used to restrict expression and then finally given the threats I'll conclude with some thoughts about how we might reinvigorate appreciation and respect for the rights to freedom of opinion and expression and that's where i'll conclude hopefully on something of an

optimistic note so first let me talk a little bit about the underlying law and many of you may already be familiar with that underlying law but so i would ask for your leave as i give a little bit of a history or little introduction to what that law is so when we're talking about human rights law related to the freedom of opinion and freedom of expression i'm

referring specifically to two sets of norms two instruments that is the Universal Declaration of Human Rights which is really the foundational instrument in international human rights law largely aspirational but it has been converted by and large to a set of binding principles in the two international covenants the International Covenant on Civil and

Political Rights the ICCPR and the International Covenant on economic Social and Cultural Rights both adopted in 1966 for our purposes tonight I'm mainly going to be making reference to the ICCPR right the International Covenant Civil and Political Rights even though its basic provision reflects and echoes the Universal Declaration of Human

Rights so what are those provisions they're really three paragraphs or four paragraphs in two separate articles of the iccpr so article 19 paragraph 1 of the iccpr protects everyone's right to hold opinions without interference article 19 paragraph 2 protects the right to seek receive and impart

information and ideas of all kinds regardless of frontiers and through any media I think that is really our fundamental principle for this evening when we're talking about freedom of expression and let me just highlight those those elements of that second paragraph of article 19 1 it's to seek it protects the right to seek receive

and impart in other words it protects our right to look for information and ideas it protects our right to receive those ideas and that information and it protects our right to express it to impart it to share it with others that's the fundamental element of the right to freedom of expression it applies

secondly to information and ideas of all kinds it's not limited to any particular kind of information it's not limited to politics or to religion or to cultural issues it's all ideas all kinds of information it's regardless of frontiers interestingly it's a right unique really in the International Covenant that applies regardless of one's borders it allows me to seek receive and impart

information from any country around the world and particularly in a digital age I think that's something that we should be focusing some of our attention on we'll talk a little bit about that hopefully later and maybe in the QA and then finally it applies to any media right at the time of the adoption of the Covenant and of the Universal Declaration so we're going back almost

70 years those who negotiated the these instruments already understood that media can change we wouldn't just be talking about newspaper or radio or television right but it would also include things that weren't invented yet like the internet now we have this right to freedom of expression and always the

question becomes well what's the ability of the state to restrict that right to express oneself and the third paragraph of article 19 provides the answer there article nineteen nineteen paragraph 3 provides restrictions on expression but not opinion and I think that's crucial opinion is unviable inviolable it cannot be restricted in any measure by any

measure or in any way but expression the expression of one's opinion may be restricted in fairly narrow circumstances and article 19 3 says that any restriction must meet a three-part test and that three-part test means one that the restriction must be clear and unambiguous an existing law right it

can't just be the decision of an executive exercising her own discretion to restrict any particular expression it has to be based on clear unambiguous law it has to be secondly focused on the legitimate purpose and it actually specifies what those legitimate purposes might be and they may be public health or order national security for the rights of reputations of others but then

finally even if the restriction is in pursuit of a legitimate objective the restriction must be necessary and proportionate to meet that objective now article 20 separate from article 19 provides for restrictions also on incitement to hostility discrimination or violence and we may talk about that

as well but those two must be subject to the three-part test that i just mentioned okay so that that should be hopefully the extent of my doctrinal presentation that would be a full class in a in a law school classroom so I want to move to the second part of the discussion which is what are the underlying principles why do we have the right to freedom of expression why do we

have the right to freedom of opinion i think it's common for for us to focus on the instrumental reasons that we have freedom of expression and i'll get to those instrumental reasons but i want to start with the freedom of expression for its own purposes the freedom of expression as a right that's untethered

to instrumental social reasons and so here is the deep question that philosophers have always struggled with and and which I think freedom of expression is actually rooted in and that is what is it that makes us distinctly human so apart from our enjoyment of reality television maybe or or cat videos on YouTube our capacity to

reason right our capacity for conscience for self-awareness and for reflection is what separates us out from the other members of the animal kingdom right reason and conscience the Universal Declaration actually celebrates reason and conscience that everyone enjoys by nature of simply being human and i think

that the freedom to exercise that reason and conscience is at the heart of the freedom of expression how is it possible to exercise reason if we lack information we lack access to information how is it possible to make decisions about our own values our identities our preferences if we lack the ability to debate them with friends

and foes alike how is it possible to form an opinion without freedom to explore in privacy our deepest or even our shallowest curiosities in short I would suggest that the freedom of expression at its core is about the freedom to be human to exercise our most fundamental human qualities of reason and conscience it is essentially a protection of human dignity just as the

prohibition of torture protects the body and the mind and the right to life protects our very existence the rights to freedom of opinion and expression protect our core human qualities were not computers to be programmed by the state and any attempt to limit the freedom of expression must be understood in this general context now so that's

not to say that freedom of expression is only that that it's only about human dignity it's also fundamental to modern human activity to democratic process and public policy debate to economic interactions and sustainable development to scientific progress and the growth of human knowledge to public health and education too tolerant pluralistic societies and the space for nonviolent

and understanding discourse of course freedom of expression and freedom of opinion allow for all of those things and are instrumental and essential for us to achieve those goals those social and political goals but it's also I think at its core about human dignity freedom of expression is very much at the core of our modern world and I would

argue that those who resist it and restrict it damage not only human freedom but their societies to enter into and prosper in contemporary life at home and internationally so third what are the threats to freedom of expression so we would not have a protection of the freedom of expression if it were not for the concern of those who actually negotiated and framed the universal

declaration of human rights in 1948 shortly after the Second World War I think it's worth reminding ourselves in a way about that moment in time when human rights law when contemporary human rights law was born right it was born in the wake of the Second World War it was born in the wake of a regime the Nazi regime in particular that initiated conflict in a variety of ways but it

bears remembering that among their first efforts among the first efforts of the Nazis was doing away with art literature and political expression that challenged National Socialist ideology the Nazi reign of terror actually began with book burnings it was the death camps that came later now of course most threats to

freedom of expression are not pathways to Gemma Seidel violence and that's that's not my point at all my point is that threats to expression are not new that the people who actually Framed the right to freedom of expression as we understand it today understood that freedom of expression would be under attack and wasn't under attack in the

past so today what marks our world of threats to expression I want to highlight several but let me make here first a preliminary remark about threats to expression I think that most denial of free opinion and expression are about maintaining a particular power structure sometimes it's about a person's power sometimes it's about party's power sometimes it's about the

power and influence of a belief or an institution where a cultural or religious norm but regardless of the kind of power sought to be maintained denial of expression has that as its name the preservation of power and this power preservation principle i think is rooted in insecurity now in security at

times may be an understandable attitude toward massive changes that modern life can impose on traditional communities but it's not a legitimate basis for governmental intervention in individual opinion and expression so how does the denial of freedom of expression manifest itself today so I think it's useful to

highlight a few current problems in two separate categories and so I want to divide this part of the discussion up between these two categories the first would be thematic or content-based restrictions on expression and the second the tools that impose those restrictions now of course this isn't

always a clear distinction between content-based restrictions and the tools to restrict but I think conceptually it allows us to think a little bit about the different threats that are out here and I do not intend to be comprehensive in discussing these current threats but I think these will be representative and then afterwards maybe this will be a

launching pad for us to talk more specifically about threats that you see as well so the first I want to talk about the first category is content or thematic restrictions which at some level can be under the umbrella also of discrimination right content-based restrictions are often about discrimination first discrimination

against vulnerable groups restrictions against the expression of vulnerable groups examples are I'll mention a few their restrictions designed to undermine for existent for instance gender or religious expression or at least where gender and religion intersect such as clothing or headscarf

coverings so for example in France there's the denial of the right to wear a headscarf whereas in some countries like Saudi Arabia and Iran the head scarf or a cut form of covering may be imposed there's ethnic expression such as education and their I'm thinking of perhaps the Baha'i in Iran where they're denied fundamental rights to education

and to ethnic heritage or ethnic expression in one's language such as restrictions on the Tibetan language in China there's LGBTI expression where there's severe restrictions on such expression and we've seen that over the last year's in places like Uganda and Russia and many other places so these

are each discriminatory restrictions on expression and they're based on restricting the expression of vulnerable groups another kind of content-based restriction is blasphemy right laws that restrict the kind of expression that one might direct toward religion and I think blasphemy laws which are prevalent throughout this region and throughout in

fact many regions and apply to all religions in many ways do more to undermine minority expression than to protect majority religious groups from harm and they become a fundamental problem for the freedom of expression not necessarily because of their intention to protect those who have

religious feeling but because they're generally used in order to the risk to restrict the expression of those who have contrary views views that vary from the mainstream religion attitude a third area of discrimination in expression restrictions on expression has to do with opposition political views repression of dissent and we see

that again in this region for example in the Sedition Act in Malaysia which even though the Prime Minister not much more than a year ago indicated that he would remove has actually used the government has actually used the Sedition Act to significant effect over the last year in order to to really intimidate opposition

and to intimidate even artists and thinkers for example the cartoonist zunar who faces up to 45 years in prison for some of his cartoons which were seen as seditious there's also the leys magis state law in thailand but not only a law that provides for restrictions on the things that we might say in thailand against the king but also across the

region and across the world there are restrictions on the kinds of things that one might say that would be interpreted as insulting the government these are content-based restrictions that ultimately undermine public debate and of course there's the vast wave of repression of expression in places like Bahrain and Egypt over the last three or

four years so these are examples of content-based restrictions on expression which by their nature are inconsistent with the freedom of expression whether they meet the three-part test for a restricting expression is another question which I think none of these actually meet but we can talk a little bit more about that in the QA perhaps so apart from those kinds of content-based

restrictions are the tools what are the tools for restricting speech today I think these tools generally fall under the category of but they come in a variety of forms and the last one that I'll get you is the one that's focused most directly on the information ages is indicated in the title of the of the lecture first we

have denial of access to information and that could include such things as the blocking of YouTube which we've seen in Pakistan or the vast firewall that blocks websites in China the blocking of social media during protests such as in Iran during the Green Revolution or even just over the past year the blocking of

access to social media in the Democratic Republic of Congo and in Burundi just over the last several months we also see as a form of censorship the targeting of journalists now of course this past year has shown us the attacks in Paris the beheadings in Syria and attacks in Colombia Mexico Ecuador Venezuela unfortunately I could go on and on the

attacks on journalists are a kind of scourge across the world today we also see the jailing of journalists in places like Myanmar China Syria Iran Egypt and elsewhere and we also see it in the in the lack of protection and attacks on protection of sources of information for journalists particularly their confidentiality where we've seen particular pressure in places like the United States then there's freedom

online freedom online in many respects should not be seen as really distinguished from in any material way from freedom offline freedom in our regular physical space it's been said quite repeatedly now particularly by my predecessor Frank LaRue but by the Human Rights Council by the UN General Assembly and by many others that rights offline apply online

it's become a kind of article of faith and it's true of course but I think that even though we see the online world as offering us kind of a vast exponential increase in our ability to have access to information to expand also exponentially the audience that we might reach with our expression the online world the digital age has also presented

governments with extensive and unprecedented abilities to track us to interfere with our privacy to interfere with our freedom of expression and and to interfere with our freedom to maintain opinions actually in ways that are much stronger and much more severe and much more restrictive of opinion and expression than we saw prior to the

digital age in other words much as we've moved so much of our communication online so too we've seen that repression has moved online as well and it's important for us to indicate exactly what that repression looks like and I would enter indicate or highlight a few areas of specific concern that I think we should all have when it comes to

freedom online so one is the argument about internet sovereignty there's there's an argument going on right now across the world around the world that internet sovereignty should be a guiding principle in other words that each country should have the ability to kind of decide for itself what its people get to see how they get to communicate with

one another what they get to communicate to one another and I think there are two problems with that so one is there's a legal problem with it because as I indicated at the beginning article 19 paragraph 2 of the ICCPR but also the Universal Declaration of Human Rights protects the right to seek receive and impart information and ideas of all

kinds regardless of frontiers so to the extent that a state wants to create a wall around its internet which is the central forum for expression in the world today they're really acting in consistently with human rights law with that ability for us to go beyond our own borders so that's I think the

fundamental legal problem with the question of Internet sovereignty but it's also a problem of technology it's simply impossible for a state today to wall itself off from the rest of the world and and I think we'll see that increasingly and we see that in China right now where it's essentially a kind of cat and mouse game when it comes to

trying to protect the great wall around China's internet and efforts inside to get access to information outside we see that in all sorts of places we see that in efforts by different governments to require that all data of individuals is maintained on servers on the territory of a particular state that websites are held on the territory of that state I

think those kinds of norms which we see emerging mainly from states that want to restrict access to formation are deeply problematic and something that those of us who are deep supporters of freedom of expression need to resist and to fight against wherever we can and the issue of internet governance which is has become an

emerging issue and is debated around the world is something that we need to be focusing our attention on separately there's both mass and targeted surveillance so just as all of our communication all of our banking all of our health information at least so much of it around the world has gone online that's opened up all sorts of avenues for governments both to collect our

information in a kind of mass way right just sweeping up all the information that we give all of the information of our searches when we do a Google search it's saved it's not anonymous generally unless although we can get to how you can do that but all of those those searches all of the information that you put out there is now subject to being

held by governments mind by governments and you are subject in a sense to losing your ability to protect your own privacy now I think that's a deep problem for privacy and a significant problem for freedom of expression because once we understand that all of our communications are susceptible to being

read and all of our social networks are susceptible to being understood by government over time our willingness to express ourselves may be undermined and we may be deterred and chilled from speaking but I think that just as critical and just as concerning are the kinds of targeted attacks that

particularly activists those who are trying to gain information those who are seeking to express them selves particularly those who are seeking to express some form of dissent and it doesn't necessarily need to be dissent against government it could be dissent against conventional thinking dissent against social mores that one

simply disagrees with increasingly those people are being targeted and surveilled for their online expression their online opinion and I think this is a significant risk for us in the digital age all of these kinds of attacks surveillance attacks on sort of the global Internet and the freedom of information digital attacks on civil

society all of these are undermined are aimed at undermining the privacy that's necessary for the exercise of opinion and expression now they're their tools to deal with this and I think those the main tools there are encryption and anonymity right the ability for us to essentially wrap our communications in a kind of cloth so that no one can read it

except your intended recipient I put a lock i scramble my data my email or my search on a website so that only the website can unscramble it or only my intended recipient can unscramble it can unlock that information that's one way that we can protect ourselves at least the content of our communication the other is anonymity and there are tools to maintain our anonymity whether

through Virtual Private Networks VPNs or through use of such tools as the Tor network or proxy servers these are going to be critical tools in an area of both mass and targeted surveillance and digital attacks they're going to be critical tools for activists who need to really access information in an environment where that information is

withheld from them and states need to be told that they should not restrict those those tools so running through much of this I think is a completely failed attempt to justify restrictions there's a failure one to provide open and transparent process of lawmaking there's a failure of substantial overbreadth and vagueness in restrictive laws themselves giving vast discretion to authorities to

restrict speech without constraint there's deeply inadequate judicial control over these restrictions and then there's the disingenuous use of permitted grounds for restrictions such as national security to repress speech and this disingenuous pneus is something that we need to fight against repeatedly and by fighting I don't mean taking up arms I mean we need to resist that

disingenuous pneus and really require States when those states restrict speech when they restrict opinion essentially require them to justify those restrictions to specify the necessity for the restriction and to justify whether the restriction itself is proportionate and I think all of these

are risks that we're facing today so I'm going to conclude with with a little bit of a focus on on this region on Southeast Asia and really just suggest because I don't think there are obvious or neat solutions for any of this but there are at least three things that I think could be done within this region

to improve the the status of freedom of expression one is states should follow the lead of countries like Indonesia and ratify the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights ratification is is critical for States both to participate in the development of human rights law but also it's a signal of

their intention to be bound by human rights law and not all states in the region have ratified it secondly there needs to be a broad process of national legal reform on all of these issues and it needs to focus not only on ensuring that the restrictions that are imposed on expression meet that three-part test under human rights law but but that

states go through and determine where they have content-based restrictions that are inconsistent with human rights law whether it's sedition or blasphemy or other discriminatory types of restrictions and then third I think for the long term the region and by the region I really mean ASEAN countries should be aiming towards a kind of regional forum to protect freedom of

expression now by that I mean really a reference to other regions around the world where regional mechanisms to protect freedom of expression and to identify problems in the implementation of the right to freedom of expression can be identified very early so there's a special rapporteur on the freedom of

expression in the inter-american system there's one in the African system there's one in the in the European system and the organization of for Security and Cooperation in Europe over the long term I think it's going to be critical for there to be a national mech and a regional mechanism for ASEAN

countries as well in order to address all of these issues so I want to conclude on a kind of hopeful note I hope so for all the threat and the risk to freedom of expression today I think we also live in an age that that's pretty remarkable in its sort of fullness of information of media platforms of ideas of images of sounds

that are really accessible to to all of us in this room and they cross borders and they inform global debate and I believe that the digital age especially provides the tools and the environment for opinion and expression well beyond what humans have known in the past it also unfortunately provides the tools for repression and that we're going to have to fight tooth and nail

but I believe the power of free expression will win out if we maintain the same commitment to freedom of expression that those who negotiated the Universal Declaration did almost 70 years ago so with that thank you and I would welcome your questions
